The Informants say that the Ingabi Marma Indjaja of Goemoelak, under the Samarang head regent, the Paoepattij Astra Widjaja, at His Highness's command, with the name Repatroema, by order of the Council Regent Natta Caesoema, who was stationed at Patterongan, was charged with gathering a quantity of rice and paddy, of which three hundred coyangs [uncertain: unit of measurement] were already stored in one house and two combongs [uncertain: unit of measurement] of paddy at Goemoelak. That the Ingabi Settjiamangalla of Torbaia, and thus the youngest brother of Demang Soeradimeja, kept them with the Chinese who were stationed at that place. That the Ingabi of Goemoelak, the aforementioned Chinese who were at Torbaya, numbering 700 men, had to be provisioned, and therefore at the toll place of Goemoelak he held [uncertain: meaning unclear]. That the Samarang head regent at the villages of Bedeede and Telagaserat "kept watch" by the rice fields that were brought there.

From Java's East Coast, the 10th of September 1741.

That a certain Cartasoerase Javanese named Bappa Paddag, the informant, would have told how the Council Regent became displeased because the Prince had taken his wife from him.

From Java's East Coast, the 16th of September 1744. Register of Papers which today are being sent from here by the ship Beekvliet to Her Excellencies, the High Indian Government at Batavia. Namely:—

No. 1: Original letter sent to the High and Esteemed Excellencies by the Esteemed and Honorable Lord Hugo Verijsel, Commissioner over Java's Northeast Coast, the Esteemed Lord Ioan Herman Theling, second in this Commission, and the provisionally appointed Regent Natta Nael Steinmetsz, together with the Council here, of today's date.

2: Two copies of letters sent by the Japanese servants from here, dated the 23rd and 24th of August last.

3: Bill of lading and invoice of the cargo loaded at Japara, brought by the bearer hereof.

4: Copy of Resolution in the War Council here, received on the 26th thereof. From Java's East Coast, dated the 10th of September 1741.

5: Request and Respectful Report by the Assistant, Resident Urban Nus Bresijn, together with an invoice of two wood rafts.

6: Council Resolution taken on the 26th of the same month. Copy of declaration by the Acting Lieutenant Que Tonko and a report made by the Under-merchant and Fiscal Jeronimus Tonnem Junior.

7: Note of settled wage accounts that are being transported with this vessel by the persons concerned.

8: Bill of lading regarding loaded powder and sugar, brought by the bearer hereof.

9: Cost account of provisions supplied to the vessel.

10: Report by Express Commissioner regarding the condition of the cargo and ships Meijenbergen and Beekvliet.

From Java's East Coast, dated the 10th of September 1744.

No. 12: Copy of Inventory of the estate of the deceased Turk Rekmatjelibe.

13: Letter sent by the Japanese servants hereward, dated the 28th of August last.

14: Copy of Resolution in the War and Political Council here, received on the 30th thereof. /Signed below/ Samarang, the 2nd of September 1741. /In the margin/ N.B. There also goes with this a separate letter addressed to Her Excellencies.

text_translated_detailed: _o From Java's East Coast under date 8 August 172 Today the 5th of October 1741 was by the undersigned Express commissioned members from the Council of Justice here and we First G Clercq in the presence of the under-Merchant Fiscal Jeronimus Tonneman Junior examined and interrogated the arrested within the Company's Lodge Lieutenant of the Chinese militia Porko who declared and made known that he consequently in the first beginning heard of the troubles by a letter sent by a Chinese Tea merchant Sionke residing at Tanjong being a supplier of the Company's rice there purchased that there gathered at that place 3 Chinese in the name Lim Torko from Coligaire Jo Tjanko from Samarang and Lim Tsipho from Batavia to reckon against the E Company which letter the confessor showed to the Mister Commandeur Visscher and the content of that made known to his Honour whereupon his Honour from Java's Post Coast under date 30 August 174n declared to him asked whether the aforesaid three Chinese each time had weapons the confessant answered his Honour that they were provided with a snaphaance [musket], pike and a shield when the Mister Commandeur said such is not yet secure with recommendation to inform himself further regarding that which having been done the confessant received by letters from said Tea merchant Sionke again notice that the rebels there had increased to 17 heads the same his Honour made known have the outcome his Honour already warned would be 700 would it still be of no consequence that the confessant proposed to his Honour the consequences that would arise from that whereupon he received from the E Company's order to write to the well-intentioned Chinese still residing at Tanjong not to merge themselves with that wicked folk within short there

text_translated_detailed: EG Clercq. To the Honorable and esteemed Mister Hugo Verijsel, Commissioner for Java's East Coast. The Noble Mister Ioan Herman Theling, Second in this Commission, and Mister Nathanael Stein, provisionally in charge, together with the council of Savat. In accordance with their High Nobility's given order by missive of the 17th of September, gentlemen concerning to proceed with the procedures against the apprehended Lieutenant of the Chinese, que Ionko, and thus over gentlemen Captain of that nation, que anko, by declaration of the 9th of May, the lieutenant accused that he was Lieutenant of many, and his stone imagery lying at Boddjong, a plot of some Chinese to gather. To prevent by the lieutenant's arrival there with this plot of the aforementioned Chinese at Semarang, saying he, Captain, heard of a matter of a Chinese here named sjong parko, the undersigned thus immediately called that Chinese and questioned him in the presence of the two expressly commissioned gentlemen whether the Captain had thus reported, to which he, Sjong planko, who regulated everything in the face of the Captain, said further. From Java's East Coast, the 24th of August 1741, nothing to prevent the Lieutenant from knowing, so that this accusation by the Captain against him, the Lieutenant, cannot be regarded as anything other than false and arising from old enmity. Furthermore, the undersigned has exactly investigated the confession recollected by him, the Lieutenant, dated the 5th of August, and testified that he could find not the slightest action to involve the aforementioned que Jonko in the criminal matter, as sustaining from the said confession that the arrested one has acquitted himself in his duty. With which I hope to have satisfied the esteemed requisition of your Honorable and esteemed gentlemen, from whom with all veneration I remain, your Honorable and esteemed obedient servant, was signed D' Tonne, man Junior, in the margin, Semarang the 24th of August 1711

text_translated_detailed: Received 22nd of September 1741. Ship Gaasperdam. From Java's East Coast, the 11th of September 1748. Batavia. To his Excellency the high esteemed Mister Adriaan Valckenier, Governor General, and the esteemed gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies. Most high and esteemed, strict, greatly honored, most earnest, manly, wise, provident, most gracious, widely commanding, and well-esteemed gentlemen. Our recent respectful letter to your high excellency and great honor has been of the date of the 2nd of this month, to which we humbly responding, have by this means to communicate two copies of resolutions taken in the war council on the 1st and 2nd of this month, containing principally that from consideration of a received report from the Javanese near Troenazonderhorig of the first of the Maksen Regent Tommagan Wiera Petra, continuing in short that twenty Tommagons with 20,600 armed Javanese and 3,500 Chinese find themselves around this head office with fourteen pieces of cannon from the conquered office Rembang and 16 from Kartasura. From Java's East Coast, the 1st of September 1741. 1895. Which are divided in their works. Item, that the enemies since then were at the Passeb erecting a high battery, to the end that by that means they could shoot into our works. With this they made preparations to make a sortie, as was also demonstrated in detail by the Captain Commandeur Mombij in a memorandum, the necessity to make a sortie on our part first, since the enemies had approached so closely that they could be reached with a pistol shot, and we therefore had no security of life, and if the enemy were to attack us, it would be within two or three days. Which was effectuated to the advantage of the Esteemed Company, of which in a subsequent letter a more detailed report will be given. Meanwhile, we in the interim, for the continuation of that expedition in the council of Police, have appointed Captains and Lieutenants Christian Benjamin Bhererten.

Meanwhile you shall successively be permitted to hold no more rice than you need for the period of five months from now, and the remainder of that grain shall be brought to us here per the Chialoup d'Blyftak, as you shall also serve to give us an account of how much rice at your Office for the strengthening of the militia there, thus to avoid our resentment and the commission which we would be forced to send afterwards. And since the 300 Inlandese militiamen for your defence there shall remain according to the esteemed order of their Honour, you shall send the ship Meijenberg to Batavia at the earliest for the satisfaction of their Honour's esteemed requisition. text_translated_detailed: 1971 From Java's East Coast, dated 11 September 1741. Translation of a Javanese letter sent by the Pangerang Adepatti, Tjacraningrat of Madura to the Merchant Vincent van Wingerden, head of the Trading Post at Surabaya, received there on 17 August and brought to Semarang on 7 September 1741. After the customary preamble: Your Honour has sent me a letter, the contents of which I have understood, and in response to this I must say that Madura cannot obtain any rice or paddy. My subjects purchased their provisions at Pasuruan and Surabaya before the war began, and that is all I have to say for this time, which is contained in this letter. (Translated by me, signed Thos Lesueur, Translator, Lower [rank]. Approved, signed In Bieler, E.G. Clercq). From Java's East Coast, dated 1 September [1741]. Translation of a Javanese letter sent by the Pangerang Adepatti, Tjacraningrat of Madura to the Heads and Chief at Surabaya, Vincent van Wingerden, received there on 30 August 1741 and brought here on 7 September 1741. After the customary preamble: In my judgment it was necessary that Radeen Ajoe aria Soeradiningraet with her people take to the field, for although she is a woman, the Sumanappers have great respect for her, especially if some Europeans went with her, even if only four men. When her people lack courage, it would also be good if the Radeen Tommagong had four Europeans with him, and with the other principal leaders two Europeans placed there, for if the superiors show courage, the common people will not flee, and if the heads dare not, those people cannot be brought to it by any force. So if Your Honour deems this advisable and approves it, I request that no time be wasted, for such delay is only harmful. (Translated by me, signed Thos Lesueur, Translator, Lower [rank]. Approved, signed J.B. Dieler, E.G. Clercq).

To the Pangerang Adepatti, Tjacraningrat: After the customary preamble: Upon receipt of Your Honour's esteemed letter of yesterday, I must report that in the last attack beyond the Ampel, over the salt river, from where we drove them out and their bintang [district], which was very strong, we had to abandon. I employed forty Europeans and three days before, at the taking of the Paseb, about twenty men. I cannot say that the Sumanappers or Pama Cassangers have more courage, being a sluggish, undisciplined lot, which is commanded by some Lascarins and the somewhat manageable soldiers of the Radeel Tommagong. The Radeel Tjaeranagara and his brothers, whose guardians they are, have also been out, but they are corrected by a certain Radeen who holds the highest authority there, which I have already corrected by word of mouth several times. The Linijs give me no small trouble, but I hope yet to bring them to order in time. In the meantime, I thank my brother for his kind advice. May you remain with the highest regard. (All that I have to say for this time is contained in this letter, which is sent to the Netherlands). Company's Trading Post at Surabaya, 29 August 1741. (Approved, signed Zoo gesw: Scribe, Lower [rank]. Approved, signed I. Baeren, C.S. Secretary). To His Excellency the Pangerang of Madura: Esteemed Title: I have the honour to congratulate my brother the Pangerang on his victory at Gresik and to thank him further for the communication regarding the posting of the Madurese in this district. I hope that Your Honour's weapons will be blessed by the Company, while I remain in great suspense here. From Java's East Coast, dated 11 September 1741. I would again undertake something of consequence, but within three or four days I cannot find the least opportunity for this, since within that time the new Command of Pasuruan must be completed, at which opportunity I would gladly have that place relieved, and for which great efforts the regents of Sumanap and Pana Cassan have agreed to let 1300 of their people be used. In the meantime, experience has taught me that one thing and another would remain stuck, so if my brother would be pleased to wait three days, I will endeavour to deliver results. I also await from my brother on what day and hour this would best suit, and I will not fail to give the proper signal for the attack. (In the meantime, all that I have to say for this time is contained in this letter, which is sent to the Netherlands). Company's Trading Post at Surabaya, 30 August 1741. (Signed V. V. Wingerden).

text_translated_detailed: From Java's East Coast under date 1 September 174[1]. We, the undersigned skipper Michiel van Son and ship's tinsmith Melis van Geldenburg and Gerrit Hessen, declare by these presents at the requisition of the Honorable Vincent van Winger, the chief merchant at this Office, having been called upon, having inspected at the wall standing here the pantjalling [a type of vessel] the Snoek, and having carefully examined and inspected the same, found that its hull is entirely rotten, completely decayed from the aforementioned keel and internally worm-eaten and deteriorated, whereby the bottom is irreparably damaged and unfit for further use. Presenting the aforementioned, which being verified, will be further executed. /understood/ Surabaya, the 1 November in the year 1741 /was signed/ Ab d' Sonhet, mark of Melis van Geldenburg, and was signed / Gerrit Hessen / Below agrees /was signed/ D[e] Baeren Clous, Secretary. Further, Honorable gentleman Vincent van Wingerden, chief merchant, 981 Java's East Coast under date 19 [September] 1741. In accordance with your Honorable and esteemed persons' order, we undersigned, as expressly commissioned, have exactly taken up and inventoried the undermentioned goods and effects of the pantjalling the Snoek, as specified stands: 8 pieces metal prime pieces 32 [pieces] hand grenades 164 lb copper [items] of 1 pound 8 [pieces] copper cartridge cases cannon grapes 32 compasses 2 76 [pieces] cartridge bags 7 [pieces] slow matches [pieces] cutlasses 12 [pieces] d[itt]o sheaths 12 560 snaplock musket balls 1 [piece] night lantern with its lamp [piece] copper fish kettle 1 1 [piece] lee hearth 1 [piece] packing 1 [piece] hard lantern 8 [pieces] gunpowder horns 1 [piece] copper powder measures 2 dredges 1 [piece] new dredge rope 1 halter, d[itt]o d[itt]o. From Java's East Coast under date 19 [September] 174[1]. 12 pieces snaplock muskets 1 [piece] scraper 1 [piece] copper cooking pan 4 [pieces] pistols 1 [piece] hood line

Translation of Javanese letter sealed to the Noble and Esteemed Gentleman Hugo Verysel and Joan Herman Theling, Commissioners on behalf of the United Dutch East India Company, on and along Java's North East Coast, together with the Noble and Esteemed Gentleman Nath. Steinmets, Lieutenant Governor of the aforementioned Coast, by the Council Member Adepatti Notta Coesoema, received on the 15th of September 1741. After the customary preamble: The last letter sent to me by you I have forwarded to Cartasoera to the Susuhunang with earnest request that his majesty, for the benefit of himself, his lands, and the Company, restore peace and forget all past matters. Item: The Company's enemies, the Chinese, to be destroyed—do not doubt that I shall apply my utmost diligence to persuade the prince thereto. But yet be mindful that I am but a servant, and therefore not in a position to pressure my Sovereign, which is not unknown to you. Therefore, this shall have to proceed slowly, so that I am not suspected by the prince, and it cannot be accomplished well within ten days, in which time I shall fully present your good intention—as for what concerns.
